title: Kubernetes 101 — Fundamentals
description: Validate your understanding of how Dynatrace monitors a Kubernetes cluster as covered in this lab: what the DynaKube and Operator do, why logs arrive without a restart, why traces require one, and how to prove each signal reached Grail.
imagine: You just finished the Kubernetes 101 enablement. The TODO app is running on a k3d cluster, monitored by Dynatrace in Application Observability mode. You want to confirm you understood *how* Dynatrace got its data — not just the kubectl commands you typed.
yourGoal: Answer questions that verify you understood what the DynaKube configures, what the Operator provisions, why log collection needed no restart while tracing did, and how to confirm each signal in Dynatrace.

story.introduction: The lab deployed the Dynatrace Operator, then a DynaKube in Application Observability mode, on a k3d cluster running a TODO app. Logs started flowing immediately; traces only appeared after a rollout restart. These questions check that you understood why.
story.context: Everything you need to answer can be found in the lab pages you just completed — especially the 'Your cluster is already capturing logs' and 'Verify the traces' sections.

questions.title: What does the DynaKube custom resource do?
questions.content: You applied a `dynakube.yaml` file in Section 2. What does the DynaKube CR tell the Dynatrace Operator?

options.text: It is a Helm values file that overrides chart defaults
options.explanation: Helm values are separate from DynaKube CRs. The DynaKube is a Kubernetes Custom Resource, not a Helm file.

options.text: It is a Kubernetes secret that stores the DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN
options.explanation: Token secrets are a separate Kubernetes Secret object. The DynaKube CR defines the desired monitoring configuration, not credentials.

options.text: It is the single source of truth for how Dynatrace monitors the cluster: which tenant to connect to, which monitoring mode to run, and which components (ActiveGate, CSI driver, log module) to provision
options.explanation: Correct! Applying the DynaKube is what made the operator provision the ActiveGate, the log-monitoring DaemonSet, and the CSI driver / webhook for code-module injection — nothing runs until the DynaKube exists.

options.text: It is a NetworkPolicy that allows traffic from the todoapp to the internet
options.explanation: NetworkPolicies are a standard Kubernetes resource. The DynaKube is a Dynatrace-specific CRD for monitoring configuration.

questions.explanation: The DynaKube CR is the control plane for Dynatrace observability. Before it existed, the operator was installed but idle. Once applied, the operator reconciled the cluster to match it: ActiveGate came up, the log module started tailing every node, and the CSI driver / mutating webhook were readied for the next pod that gets created.
hints: Re-read the intro of Section 2 — 'Without a DynaKube, the operator is installed but idle.'
Think of the DynaKube like a deployment spec: it describes desired state, and the operator makes it happen.

questions.title: Why did logs arrive without restarting the todoapp?
questions.content: The `todoapp` had been running since before the DynaKube was ever applied, yet its logs showed up in Grail without any restart or code change. Why?

options.text: The log-monitoring module runs as a DaemonSet that tails the standard output of every container already running on the node — it works entirely from outside the application process
options.explanation: Correct! One log-monitoring pod per node reads the log files the container runtime already writes to disk. It never touches the application process, so pods don't need to be recreated for logs to start flowing.

options.text: The todoapp was coded to push its logs directly to the Dynatrace API
options.explanation: The lab explicitly calls out 'no change to your application — no logging library, no sidecar, no log driver'.

options.text: Kubernetes automatically restarted the todoapp pods when the DynaKube was applied
options.explanation: Applying a DynaKube does not trigger restarts of unrelated workloads in other namespaces.

options.text: OneAgent was already injected into the todoapp before the lab began
options.explanation: The lab states the todoapp 'has never been restarted or instrumented' at that point — injection requires the mutating webhook, which only fires on pod creation.

questions.explanation: Log collection needs no application restart, no code injection, and no change to your application — the log-monitoring DaemonSet reads container log files from the node itself. That is fundamentally different from how traces are captured, which is why the very next section required a restart.
hints: The lab page title is literally 'Your cluster is already capturing logs'.
Logs come from outside the process; traces come from inside it.

questions.title: Why do pods need a restart to produce traces?
questions.content: In Section 3 you ran `kubectl rollout restart deployment -n todoapp` before any trace data appeared. Why is a restart required for tracing but not for logging?

options.text: The Dynatrace Operator needs a reboot to activate its licence
options.explanation: Dynatrace licensing is not tied to pod restarts.

options.text: Tracing requires the OneAgent code module to run inside the application process itself, and the mutating webhook can only inject it at the moment a pod is created — pods already running before the DynaKube existed never passed through that webhook
options.explanation: Correct! Distributed tracing needs code-level visibility into the running process. That code module is delivered by the CSI driver and wired in by the mutating webhook, which only intercepts pods at creation time — so existing pods must be recreated to be instrumented.

options.text: Kubernetes requires a full cluster restart whenever a new CRD is installed
options.explanation: CRDs extend the API without requiring cluster or pod restarts.

options.text: The todoapp needs to re-read a DT_ENVIRONMENT variable from a ConfigMap to enable tracing
options.explanation: Environment variables alone don't instrument an application — the agent's code module must be injected into the running process by the webhook.

questions.explanation: Logs are read from outside the process (log files on the node), so no restart is needed. Traces require the agent to run inside the process, and Dynatrace injects that agent via a mutating webhook that only fires when a pod is created — so a rollout restart is the only way to get already-running pods instrumented.
hints: Think about when Kubernetes calls a mutating webhook — only at pod creation.
The annotation `oneagent.dynatrace.com/injected: true` only appears on pods that went through the webhook after the DynaKube existed.

questions.title: How do you confirm OneAgent was injected into a pod?
questions.content: After restarting the todoapp pods, what is the most direct way to confirm that the OneAgent code module was successfully injected?

options.text: Check that the pod carries the annotation `oneagent.dynatrace.com/injected: "true"`, stamped by the mutating webhook at pod creation
options.explanation: Correct! This annotation is the definitive local proof of injection — it is exactly what the lab's shell validation (`checkOneAgentInjected`) checks for.

options.text: Look for a new container named `oneagent` running inside the pod
options.explanation: Application Observability mode injects a code module via an init container and shared volume — it does not add a permanent running sidecar container.

options.text: Check that the pod's CPU usage doubled after the restart
options.explanation: OneAgent has minimal CPU overhead; CPU usage is not a reliable injection indicator.

options.text: The Dynatrace Operator logs will print 'injection complete' for each pod
options.explanation: Injection is handled by the mutating webhook at admission time, not printed by the operator controller — the evidence lives in the pod annotation.

questions.explanation: The annotation `oneagent.dynatrace.com/injected: "true"` is stamped by the Dynatrace mutating webhook at pod admission time. It is the canonical, local proof that the agent was injected — before you ever go looking for traces in Grail.
hints: The lab's shell validation for Section 3 checked this exact annotation.
Run `kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n todoapp` and look at the Annotations section.

questions.title: How do you verify a log reached Dynatrace?
questions.content: After adding a todo, which DQL query correctly verifies that its log line reached Grail, scoped to your own cluster session?

options.text: fetch logs, from:now()-15m | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}") | filter contains(content, "Adding a new todo")
options.explanation: Correct! `fetch logs` reads the logs data lakehouse table, and `endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, ...)` scopes results to your unique cluster session so classmates sharing the tenant don't pollute each other's results.

options.text: fetch spans, from:now()-15m | filter k8s.namespace.name == "todoapp"
options.explanation: `fetch spans` queries distributed traces, not logs — it would not surface the log content produced by the app.

options.text: kubectl logs -n todoapp deployment/todoapp | grep Grail
options.explanation: That only shows local container stdout — it does not confirm the data reached the Dynatrace Grail backend.

options.text: fetch logs, from:now()-15m | filter k8s.cluster.name == "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}"
options.explanation: An exact `==` match fails because Kubernetes truncates long cluster names — the training-name prefix gets cut, but the session id at the end survives. `endsWith` is required.

questions.explanation: Logs live in the `logs` data lakehouse table. `fetch logs` combined with `endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}")` and a content filter is exactly what the lab used to prove the log-monitoring module shipped your todo's log line — with zero code changes to the app.
hints: Logs and traces live in different DQL tables: `logs` vs `spans`.
Remember why the lab used `endsWith` instead of `==` on `k8s.cluster.name`.

questions.title: How do you verify a trace reached Dynatrace?
questions.content: After adding a todo (post-restart), which DQL table do you query to confirm the injected agent captured a distributed trace for that request?

options.text: fetch logs
options.explanation: `fetch logs` reads log lines, not distributed traces — traces are a separate signal captured by the injected code module.

options.text: fetch spans
options.explanation: Correct! `fetch spans, from:now()-15m | filter endsWith(k8s.cluster.name, "{{DT_SESSION_ID}}")` surfaces the `POST /todos` root span recorded by OneAgent from inside the running process — the signal that did not exist before the restart.

options.text: fetch events
options.explanation: Events capture things like deployments or problems, not per-request distributed traces.

options.text: fetch metrics
options.explanation: Metrics are aggregated numeric time series, not individual request traces with span names and endpoints.

questions.explanation: Traces are recorded as spans by the code module running inside the instrumented process, and queried with `fetch spans`. Each span carries the same `k8s.cluster.name` / `k8s.namespace.name` / `k8s.workload.name` context as the logs — that shared metadata is what lets Dynatrace stitch Kubernetes identity onto every signal, and what let you scope the query to your own cluster.
hints: This is 'the signal that did not exist before the restart' — recheck the 'Verify the traces' section.
Traces are made of spans; a root span here is named `POST /todos`.

questions.title: What does the ActiveGate do?
questions.content: After applying the DynaKube, an ActiveGate pod started in the `dynatrace` namespace. What is its role in getting logs and traces from your cluster to Dynatrace?

options.text: It is the Kubernetes API server proxy that the operator uses to watch for CRD changes
options.explanation: The operator connects to the Kubernetes API server directly — the ActiveGate is not involved in that path.

options.text: It acts as a secure gateway that routes observability data (logs, traces, metrics) collected in the cluster to your Dynatrace tenant
options.explanation: Correct! The ActiveGate is a local routing proxy: the log module and the injected agents send their data to it, and it securely forwards everything to the Dynatrace SaaS backend.

options.text: It stores all collected data locally so the cluster works without internet access
options.explanation: The ActiveGate forwards data onward to the tenant; it is not a permanent offline data store.

options.text: It injects the OneAgent code module into application pods
options.explanation: That is the job of the CSI driver and mutating webhook, not the ActiveGate.

questions.explanation: The ActiveGate is the local relay between everything running in your cluster (log module DaemonSet, injected code modules) and the Dynatrace tenant. Both the logs and the traces you verified in Grail traveled through it.
hints: Think about the data path: log module / injected agent → ? → Dynatrace tenant.
The ActiveGate sits between the components you deployed and the Dynatrace backend.

learningObjectives: Explain what the DynaKube custom resource configures and why the operator does nothing without one
Explain why log collection requires no restart or code change to the application
Explain why distributed tracing requires a pod restart after the DynaKube is applied
Identify the pod annotation that confirms OneAgent code-module injection
Write a DQL query to verify logs reached Grail, scoped to your cluster session
Write a DQL query to verify traces (spans) reached Grail
Describe the role of the ActiveGate in routing observability data to the Dynatrace tenant
